units.text: B. Glossary: words that change the question
Empirical adequacy. A theory’s ability to correctly represent relevant observable phenomena. It is not by definition identical to the complete truth of its ontology.
Anisotropy. Dependence of a property on direction. An observed anisotropy requires explaining source, propagation and measurement before attributing it to a fundamental structure.
Causality. The relationship through which some changes matter for producing others. Philosophical definitions and identification methods differ; mere correlation does not alone fix causal direction.
Initial condition. Description of the state from which we apply an evolution rule. Information placed here must not be confused with information explained by the rule.

Dimensionless constant. A quantity whose numerical value does not depend on unit choice. It is particularly important when asking whether physical relationships, rather than measurement conventions, have changed.
Counterfactual. A statement about what would happen in a situation different from the actual one. Laws are often used for such questions, not merely to summarize the past.
Decoherence. A process through which interaction with the environment makes certain interference locally inaccessible. It does not in itself presuppose a conscious observing mind.
Determinism. A model property in which the relevant state and rules determine a unique evolution. It is not synonymous with practical predictability.
Domain of validity. The set of conditions under which a relationship can be used with the stated precision. An approximation can be excellent within its domain and inadequate outside it.
Weak emergence. The appearance of collective behaviors from basic interactions without postulating additional fundamental powers. Novelty of description does not imply violation of the mechanism.
Strong emergence. A family of positions holding that a whole introduces properties or powers irreducible in an ontological sense. This is a stronger thesis than computational difficulty.
Epistemology. The study of knowledge, justification and their limits. ‘How can we know?’ is not identical to ‘what exists?’
Deterministic chaos. Behavior in which sensitivity to initial conditions can severely limit predictions although the rule introduces no fundamental randomness.
Identifiability. The ability to distinguish models or parameters through accessible observations and interventions. More data of the same type do not resolve every lack of identifiability.
Induction. The passage from observed cases to more general or future expectations. Its practical usefulness is not a deductive guarantee of nature’s uniformity.
Effective law. A relationship formulated for particular scales and relevant variables that need not describe every detail of the underlying mechanism.
Statistical law. A relationship about distributions, frequencies or collective values. A rare individual outcome can be compatible with the law; specified probabilities matter.
Metalaw. A proposed rule for how other rules are established or modified. Explanation at this level does not automatically close the question of foundations.
Model. A selective representation constructed for a purpose. It can combine laws, approximations, conventions and assumptions about conditions.
Nomological necessity. What is necessary relative to a world’s laws. It must not be confused with logical necessity, where the alternative would produce a contradiction.
Ontology. Inquiry into what exists and existence’s fundamental categories. The same predictions can be compatible with different ontologies.
Explanatory reductionism. The idea that one level’s explanation can be obtained from a more basic level’s description. It differs from the thesis that everything has a physical substrate.
Symmetry. A transformation leaving a model’s relevant structure unchanged. It is not reducible to a drawing’s visual symmetry.
State / rule. The state describes the system’s situation; the rule specifies relationships or transformations. Changing state does not automatically change the rule.
Underdetermination. A situation in which available evidence is compatible with multiple explanations. It may be temporary or persist for every accessible observation.
Universality. In collective-system studies, the appearance of common behaviors in different microscopic mechanisms under specified conditions. It does not mean every detail is irrelevant.
Likelihood. The probability of data under a specified model. It is not the same as the model’s probability after observing the data.
